utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were members of the El Mujahed Detachment, Arabs, and we were there from time to time, and the El Mujahed Detachment command was also there, as was the outpatients' clinic and some other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, finally, sir, do you know the time period when you saw Abu Isa in the Vatrostalna building?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I'm sure I saw him. I think it was 1995. I can't be sure, but 1995, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, PW-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question in regard to the cross-examination of yesterday. I am sorry to ask you the question today only, but yesterday you spoke, Witness, about an incident, an armed incident, concerning someone called "Ramo Durmis" in your detachment. I simply would like to know, with regard to that incident that you described to us in detail yesterday, was an investigation carried out?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Ramo Durmis, he was not a member of the detachment. This incident occurred when we were -- I don't know whether it was Muslimanske Snage or the 7th Muslim. I don't know. But it was in Visoko after an action, the action to deblock Sarajevo, in fact. And I think that they were prosecuted, but that did not happen until the end of the war. Something like that. I don't know. I think that they did have some problems, but I really can't tell you now what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these prosecutions or this prosecution, you said, took place after the war. Were they criminal proceedings, or disciplinary proceedings, or was it an administrative procedure? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I know that they did have some problems, and they were supposed to be held responsible. I know that they complained later that somebody had come looking for them because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge? I have just a few. You first, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after you conclude your examination, I wanted to ask a question that arose from Judge Lattanzi's question. I didn't realise that you had some questions, yourself. I apologise for standing up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Mr. PW-2, where is the Krajina in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Which part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krajina is in northwestern part of Bosnia. It borders with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, is that a Bosnian Krajina or was it a Serb Krajina, or is there any difference between them? Are there two such Krajinas.

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Bosnian Krajina. This is its official name, Bosanska Krajina, Bosnian Krajina. As for the Serb Krajina, it is in Croatia. We didn't actually call that "Krajina" at that time. The Serbs called that "Krajina" when they had this armed conflict with Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Vahidin, was he a member of the shura?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we can just go back to the certificate that was shown to you a little earlier during cross-examination, which relates to what soldiers were given at the end of the war and that some people were selling because they were worthless. You said, at page 41, lines 19 to 25, that these certificates were also given to the HVO, am I right, and I guess also the HOS?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these were given by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I understand?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do I understand you to say that they were also given to the HVO, against whom the army of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had fought?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How was that possible, to commend your enemies?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise to be saying this, but if anyone had asked me, I would not have given them anything. But that's politics for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I want to understand that politics. Will you please make me understand that politics?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I really can't do that, because I find it impossible to understand how they could be given the certificates when they fought us; not us, but Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I really can't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You understand that that's politics for me. I would like you to explain this politics which I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to say something. The conflicts between the BH Army and the Croatian Defence Council, or rather, the Croat forces stopped once the Washington Agreement was signed, and that's when the Croats agreed to be part of an alliance, in a way, with the BH Army, its allies. They recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was the gist of it. So an agreement was signed between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, why this period while they actually fought against the BH Army was counted in their favour, to their credit, when those certificates were issued, I don't know. Probably that was one of the terms in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry. I'm going to be with you for some time on this point. You will understand that I don't understand the politics there, so I would like to understand. Surely, sir, the very question you're asking yourself at the very end of your answer is very pertinent. Just how does the Bosnian government commend the HVO for a period when they were enemies? That they have signed an agreement in Washington can explain why they become allies from that time onwards, but surely the Croatian government could give similar certificates to members of the HVO instead of such certificates coming from the Bosnian government. Don't you think so? Does it make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for Croatia, Croatia is a different country. It's a different state, and it shouldn't really have anything to do -- it should not be interfering with Bosnia-Herzegovina, even when it comes to ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is my point precisely, that it seems as if the Bosnian government is interfering with the Croats and giving them commendations. Why didn't the government of -- if this was as a result of an agreement, why did the Croatian government not also give such similar certificates to members of t of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the real goal of this agreement was to put an end to the hostilities. That was the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I agree with you there. That would be the most important purpose of any agreement. What I don't understand is why, as a result of such an agreement, such commendations should be given and not reciprocated by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. You say you really don't know, sir. So in fact, at the end of the day, you are not able to give an explanation for the commendations to the HVO by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know is that Croats had this very strong influence, both in military and in economic terms. So the reason why an agreement was signed in that form was to ensure that the situation remained stable, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem, Witness, is that you keep harping on the agreement. My questions relate to the commendations, to the certificates. Why would a government give commendation certificates to members of an army against whom that government was fighting? That's the question I'm asking. Forget about the agreement.

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said. When I heard that the HVO members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, don't repeat. If you don't have anything new to tell me, just tell me you don't know. I don't want you to repeat yourself. Okay. Thank you very much. You are obviously not able to answer my question. Any questions arising from the Bench's questions, starting with the Prosecution? Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me see if I can get an answer that might help shed some light on the questions the Presiding Judge put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: PW-2, the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, was that military organisation made up of Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Aren't you putting words into his mouth? Why don't you ask him who was it made up of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, who the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, was made up of, the nationality of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's water under the bridge. He's answered you already. Get on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's the only question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Questions from you, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just make one thing certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the HVO received those certificates?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That members of the HVO received those certificates?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know why?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, sir. You said, in response to a question by Judge Lattanzi, you mentioned Ramo Durmis and some investigations, but you don't know why Ramo Durmis was on trial after the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he was tried. I know that he was a person prone to causing problems. He was always a very specific character.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you can't establish any link between this incident and his trial?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the trial. I know that he was prone to problems. That was not the only incident that he was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So there were other criminal acts or activities that could be linked with crimes?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was always a trouble-maker. I wasn't really interested in learning the details. I just know that he was a trouble-maker.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Sir, this brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you for taking the time to come and testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My understanding is we're scheduled to break at 12.00. Maybe we can take the recess now, reconvene at 12.20, and sit for an hour straight. But I'm entirely in your hands on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take the break now and come back at 20 past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, and Good afternoon to you, sir. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My colleague, Laurie Sartorio will be leading this witness, and I would also like to put on the record that we are being assisted by our intern, Sarai Jacob, for this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Sartorio. MS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Berislav Marijanovic, and I was born in the village of Paklarevo in the Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The Travnik Municipality of the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, could you tell us what the ethnic composition was of your village?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was an ethnically-pure Croat village. The village of Paklarevo is located between Turbe and Travnik. And it is below Mount Vlasic, and there is a location by the name of Galica. And then in 1992, in late March, that's where the Serb army came, and they dug in their. They dug their trenches there, while we had some kind of civilian protection set up around the village, because we wanted to prevent them from getting into the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you a couple more questions, if you don't mind, just to back up a second. Were you ever in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1986, and I left in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then were you ever a member of any other military organisation or any type of village patrol?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the civilian village guards in 1992, all the way up to the 15th of May. When shells started coming in from Galica, I was seriously wounded because a shell impacted behind me. And I was transferred to the hospital in Travnik, and I was hospitalised for ten or 11 days there; and then when I was discharged --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Thank you for telling us. I need you to tell the Chamber, briefly, what the atmosphere was like where you were living at that time, in terms of any type of whether military conflicts were starting; and if so, by which groups?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the atmosphere, the relations between the Croats and the Muslims was good. The atmosphere was good, but Serbs attacked both Croats and Muslims from Mount Vlasic, Turbe, Paklarevo, and all the villages around it. So we faced the same aggressor. They attacked both of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, at this time, you were part of a -- were you part of any type of Croatian military organisation, formal military organisation?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the civilian protection. I had my pistol. That was my personal property, and I went there to stand guard around the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you say "civilian patrol," did the patrol consist of both Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sir, just -- I beg your pardon. Your Honour, sorry to interrupt. I think it prudent just to mention - I'm sure it's not disputed - my learned friend, the Prosecutor, was referring to Croatian military organisations and Croats and Muslims. I don't think it's in dispute between the parties that what we're talking about is Bosnian Croats, and I just thought that helpful to mention at this stage, just to clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Does that help, Madam Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of 1993, where were you living at that time?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the first time that I was wounded and after I left the hospital, I went to the village of Maline because I was married from the village of Maline, and that's where I lived until the 8th of June, 1993, when the conflict between Croats and Muslims erupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Prior, during the time that you lived in Maline up until the 8th of June, which is the date that you just mentioned, did you ever encounter or see anyone who later became known to you or at that time became known to you as the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'd see some groups in Travnik, at Mehuric, too, because there was a village fair down there every Wednesday. So I did see those small groups because I was able to tell. Because of their language and because of the colour of their skin, I was able to tell them apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was there anything else about them that was a distinguishing feature?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of them walked around in camouflage uniforms. They wore beards. They talked different from us locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, what, if anything, had you heard at that time about the presence of the Mujahedin in the area, what your understanding was of what they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had not come there -- well, they had come there to fight. I didn't know who they wanted to fight, but I was sure that they were there to fight someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to direct your attention to the 8th of June of 1993, and ask you where you were in the very early morning of that day.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, in the early morning hours, I was in my wife's brother's house. This is where my family was. And then between 4.00 and 5.00 a.m., there was an artillery attack on the village of Maline. It was launched by the Muslim army. And then after this artillery attack, we could hear a lot of infantry fire, and it lasted for some considerable time, until they managed to take the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you mean by "considerable time"? Approximately, how many hours do you recall that this conflict went on?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The conflict started in the morning and went on for about ten hours. It went on until the afternoon, until the civilians left towards Mehuric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you,, sorry. And until that point, when you mentioned the civilians left, did you stay in your house the entire time?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the house with my family. When the shelling began, we went to the cellar. It wasn't just me and my family, but also my wife's brother and children. We were all in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt. I thought I heard the witness say this attack was by a Muslim army, was launched by a Muslim army. What do you mean by "a Muslim army"? That's at page 63, line 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: From being inside your house, were you able to see anything outside the windows, what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw two or three stables burning, a house, people shouting, "Allahu Akbar" around the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We saw soldiers shouting for us to get out of our houses. When we came out of our houses and surrendered to them, I had my pistol which I handed over to a soldier. We all left the cellar, and that was when I saw the soldiers. They were walking around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And, approximately, how many soldiers did you see walking around in the area of your house?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where we came out of the house, there were three or four of them, but they came and went.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you recall what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms. On their shoulders, they had white ribbons, probably some sort of insignia, and they had black bandanas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, after you came out of your house, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we left the house, we surrendered. We all gathered together, and then we sent out on the road towards Mehuric. They took us in the direction of Mehuric, a group of 40 or 50 civilians, and I was among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would like to bring up Map number 10, if possible, and for the witness to look at and to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to come up on the screen, in terms of the composition of the group, were there women in this group?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were women, there were children, there were elderly, soldiers, a mixed group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And were there also some persons such as yourself who were of military age who had joined the group voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for example, my wife's brother, his son. And there were other people I didn't really know, but they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were any persons in your group dressed in any type of a military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my group at that time, no, not in my group of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So we now have the map up. I would like you to draw a number"1" or write a number "1", where the group, this group of 50 or so you had mentioned, had collated, gotten together.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's Gornje Maline and this is Donje Maline. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And your group started out where, at Gornje?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: From Gornje Maline, where I put number 1, that was where the first group was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did the group, at this point, start walking?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told us to go in the direction of Mehuric under Bikosi and Poljanice, and to take the road towards Mehuric. When we got to below Bikosi --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Sorry. Who is "they"? Was someone leading your group?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The BH Army was leading the group. There was three or four soldiers there, and up there we came across a Mujahedin who couldn't speak Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And this is what you were just going to tell us. Just beneath Bikosi, you can explain to the Chamber now what happened.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we got to below Bikosi, we found -- we came across a Mujahedin who had a Golf 1, a white one. He didn't turn on the engine. He selected three of us to push the car to a part where he could go on his own, and we pushed the car. When we stopped pushing it, he went off on his own, and we rejoined our column. And we went through the village of Poljanice in the direction of Mehuric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could I stop you, please? Could you put a number "2" where you had this event with a vehicle, please?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, just a question. Did you notice if anyone in your group, in the group that you were walking with, not the soldiers who were escorting you but your group, was anyone carrying a fire-arm, that you could tell?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of them had long barrels, rifles, and there was even one sniper escorting us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking about the civilians that you described or the men, women, and children in your group.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: None of the civilians did. I had my own personal pistol which I had handed over to that soldier, who had the sniper. And my wife's brother had his own personal pistol and he handed it over just as I did, in the village before we set out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you notice anyone else who handed over any weapons in the village before you headed out?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was just our group. They said, "If you don't hand over your weapons, we will kill you." So it was better to hand them over than get killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question to you, sir, is: Did you notice anybody else in your group, other than yourself and your brother-in-law, who handed over a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see anybody else, apart from the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, after you left the spot at number 2, where did your group head?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We went towards the village of Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you reach the village of Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We reached the village of Poljanice and went through in the direction of Mehurici. When we were close to Mehurici, a column that had set out before ours were there, and some young men had already been separated off from that column and were being taken back towards the village of Maline, towards Bikosi. They were going back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to stop you here for a moment. And, please, could you mark on the map with a number "3" where what you just described happened, where you met up with another group?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I need you to explain just a little bit more clear what you just said; in other words, when you got to that spot, you -- did you meet up with another group?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We met up with this other group, which -- well, these young men, the oldest were about 45, had already been separated out from that group of civilians. They stopped next to our group. I was carrying my little son. He was four or five months old, and my four-year-old son was walking beside me. A soldier approached me. He snatched the child from me and gave it to my wife in order to pull me out and get me to join that column which was going back. And they did the same to my wife's brother and some other youngish men, Croats from the neighbouring villages. I didn't know them that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I just need to ask you about the group that you met up with. You said that they had -- I believe you said that they had already been separated, and they were heading back toward Maline. How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Because those civilians who had gone before us were not going back. It was just these young men who have been separated out from those civilians. They were heading back. They stopped next to our group, and then they pulled us out of our group and put us together with them, and then we set out towards Poljanice, towards Bikosi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About how many of these young men were there who were separated from the other group, more or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were between 15 and 19. I don't know exactly, around 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And how many from your group were separated to join that group, that group of young men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six, seven who joined their group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So then six from your group to join them. Thank you very much, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you know anyone from that group that you met?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew Zdravko Pranjes. He was from the village of Maline. I knew him. We had come across each other. We weren't on close terms or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone else from that group, other than this person?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, not in that group. No, I didn't know them that well. I knew people by sight, but I didn't really know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, at the point where the number of you were taken from your group to join that group, can you tell us who was escorting the group at that point, what types of persons?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Escorting that group, Mujahedin and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the local people or the people from Bosnia were wearing camouflage uniforms, and they had stockings over their heads with slits for the eyes, like ninjas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why it's your belief that they were the local Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson is on his feet. Just a second, sir. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would be grateful if my learned friend could rephrase that question, because in her last question she referred to the local Muslim soldiers. That terminology has not been used so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I will rephrase the question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, you just -- you stated a minute ago that the persons were with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that you believe that they were in that army, the ones that had the ninja masks that you mentioned. Can you tell us why you believe that they were with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They had insignia showing that they were members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were wearing masks because these young men from those villages who had grown up among them would recognise them. That's why they wore those masks. They were from neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you hear them speaking?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They talked among themselves, yes. They were talking among themselves. I didn't hear what about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you hear what language they were speaking, if you knew?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Some spoke in a language I didn't understand; probably Arabic, a language that hasn't been used in our parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm talking about the men with the masks, whether you are able to tell the Chamber whether you recognised the language they were speaking.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were speaking Croatian, like me. While there was Yugoslavia, we used to call the language "Serbo-Croatian." Those in the camouflage uniforms spoke the same language I did. The Mujahedin did not wear masks. Their faces were exposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when the Mujahedin spoke, did you recognise their language?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. All they could say to us was "Bojovnik" and "Ustasha Bojovnik," meaning the Croat word for "Fighter." But when they spoke among themselves, I couldn't understand their language.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now can you please tell us where the group started to go?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That group set out towards the village of Poljanice, back towards Bikosi. Shall we mark it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. You can mark where you walked to next, if you don't mind, with a "5," please -- Oh, no, "4." Sorry.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just say, while we were going towards Poljanice, between the place we were separated off and Poljanice, we met a girl who was walking with her aunt. She was wearing a camouflage uniform, and she had a Red Cross armband. Her name was Ana Pranjes, and her aunt was there, whose nickname was Turka [phoen]. I knew them. A soldier approached her and told her to take off her armband. She refused to do so, then a Mujahedin approached her. She was wearing a chain around her neck. He tore off the chain. She probably had a cross on the chain. He threw it away, the cross, and he put the chain into her -- into his pocket; then he tore off her armband and made her join our column.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you please mark a "4" where this event happened?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this, sir: Was anyone in your group, not the escorts, not the army, the soldiers from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but did anyone in your group become belligerent or argumentative at all during this time?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, no. I just remember that one soldier said, "Now we've taken your shrine at Guca Gora. We'll burn it." He said that to the other one, and the other one said, "I'm not interested in that."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, what happened next, if anything?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The column moved on towards Poljanice; and when we arrived in Poljanice, we met a group of wounded, four or five of them, and four or five others who were assisting them, because some had crutches, others had sticks, and so on. And there was a woman who had been wounded in the leg the day before. She was about 60 years old. She was on a stretcher. And they sent back that group of wounded with us to the village of Bikosi. When we set out from there, a BH Army soldier told me that someone had been shot through both legs, and they had used a wooden fence to carry him, and he told me to take over and carry him with three others. I carried him through a wooded area. We got out onto a meadow where there were BH Army trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you please mark a "5" on the map where this event happened, where you picked up the wounded soldier?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I need to ask you, when you say you came upon a group of wounded, could you describe, other than the woman you described, were the rest of the group men, were they soldiers, were they civilians, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were soldiers. The brother of one of them had been wounded, and they two others were helping him because his leg was shattered. They were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Soldiers from what force?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could you just tell us briefly, is Poljanice a village or is it an area? Can you please describe to the Judges what it is?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a small village, a hamlet called Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, what happened next, sir?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We left Poljanice. I was carrying Srecko Bobas. The group stopped on a meadow, and on the meadow were BH Army trenches. The column stopped. About 12 men were separated off from the first group and made to stand next to the trenches. They stood there in a row in front of the trench. There were three or four of them, a Mujahedin and three locals. And there was some sort of misunderstanding among them, because I thought they would kill someone us right there on that spot. They discussed something and then they sent that group back to our column, and we went on towards Bikosi two by two. When we set out towards Bikosi, another four were carrying Srecko Bobas behind me. I wasn't carrying him anymore at that point, because this man had issued an order that another four men should carry him. The column moved towards Bikosi. We stopped for a while below Bikosi, and then we set out again. It was a brief stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I stop you briefly. Could you please mark with the number "6" where the stop was by the trenches?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And now could you mark with a "7" where you just mentioned this brief stop occurred?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may continue with what occurred next.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The group walked on towards the village of Bikosi. To the left, there was a road leading to Maline, but we went straight ahead. Bikosi is a little hamlet behind Maline. When we got to the houses, on the right-hand side were two stables, on the left-hand side were houses. There were wooden fences on both sides, the left and the right. The road was an asphalt road. When we arrived at the point between the stables and the houses, Mijo Tavic had an attack. He had a fit. He was ill. He suffered from epilepsy, and he had an epileptic fit. He started shouting out. And when he yelled out, I turned around to tell the BH Army soldier that this man was ill, but they opened bursts of fire right away. The one that was shooting next to me held his rifle low down. He was shooting towards the asphalt, but he wounded me in my left leg. When I saw people falling down, I put my hands on my head and I fell down towards the right. I lay down on the asphalt. I kept quiet, and I peeped out through my fingers. On the right-hand side, there was a fence. And an HVO soldier was jumping over the fence and he was shot, and he remained lying over the fence. The BH Army soldier behind me who was shooting, he shouted out, and he said that he was wounded in the stomach because probably had a bullet had ricocheted off the asphalt. He shouted out, too, and I didn't dare raise my head anymore. I lay quietly until they started walking among us and shooting people in the head one by one. I thought I would not survive this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need to ask you a couple of questions. When you say there was -- when the firing started, can you tell me, was it a burst of fire or was it single shots?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: At first, there were bursts, as many bullets -- a hail of fire, as many bullets as they could fire. And then once the bursts stopped, then there were individual shots, and you could hear the wounded people moan. And I assumed that when we could hear those isolated shots, they didn't go in any order, because the man next to me was shot in the head and I was splattered by the blood from his head. And I hunkered down because I was waiting for the bullet to come, but he left me alone; and then they would just fire those isolated shots. So I just lay there maybe ten minutes. I don't know how long it took because I was terrified and all. I was silent, and then all of a sudden I could hear this voice saying, "Help. Is there anyone alive here? I've been wounded." I waited a little while because I was afraid there would be some more shooting; and when no more shots came, I put my head up and I saw that some people leapt up, so I did, and I was amazed to see there were some people still alive. I leapt over a fence that was to my right, although I was wounded; and then I ran down to the -- through the meadows to the left. And to the right there was a Vranjaca hill, there was a large amount of troops, and they started firing on me and the four people running behind me. We were running towards the village Podstinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you, sir? Thank you. I need to take you back a bit where you said that an HVO soldier jumped over the fence. Okay. Can you tell us where, if the fence was in front, or behind you, or on the side, and whether when this person what you saw, did he run before the firing started?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The fence was to my right; and as I fell down, I was very close to the fence, my head was close to it. And my hands were on my eyes, so I just peeked through my fingers. And during the shooting, the bursts, he tried to jump over it and he was shot, and he remained lying there over the fence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether, when he had run away or started to run away, whether he was running towards anyone who was shooting at him?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: He couldn't run anywhere because the fence was right there. He wanted to jump over the fence in order to save his life. Had he been able to do so, he would have survived, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you please put an "8" on the map where this event occurred, please?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could you please describe to the Judges the route you took and how long it took you to reach safety, and then what happened?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were moving from Bikosi towards Podstinje, that's a village. I was fleeing towards the village, and the other four were fleeing behind me. And when they caught up with me, there was a young man, Zeljo Puselja from Podavi. I knew him by sight, and we went with him to a meadow further down from Podstinje. There were some trees there, and we tried to dress our wounds. A man, young man had a wound. He was wounded in the ribs. So I stripped my vest, because it was not really cold, and we used my vest to bind our wounds. A man by the name of Puselja was hit in the left hip, I think, and this young boy who was with me, I think he was not wounded at all. A bullet just went very, very close to him and singed him. And there's a river called Bila that flows next to Mehuric. One man wearing civilian clothes and one man wearing military clothes came out of the water, and they said, "Surrender, lie down. It's over." And I immediately started running. The kid ran after me. So we ran to the left and then we crossed Bila, and we ran towards Fazlic, crossing the road leading to Mehuric. And near the village of Fazlici, about 500 metres -- from a distance of about 500 metres, two bursts were fired at us, and then we went to right to the village of Orasac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I stop you for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just need some clarification here. You said at page 78, line 1: "A man, a young man, had a wound. He was wounded in the ribs. So I stripped my vest, because it was not really cold, and we used my vest to bind our wounds." Then you also say: "A man by the name of Puselja was hit in the right hip, I think, and this young boy that was with me," now, I imagine you're referring now to Zeljo, "he was not wounded at all." I'm not sure. First, you said he was injured in the rib. Now you say he was not wounded at all. What was actually the correct situation at that point? Was he wounded or was he not wounded?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Darko Puselja was wounded in the shoulder and the rib area. Zeljo Puselja was wounded in the arm, close to the elbow, through the elbow. All four of us were wounded. Just the kid was not wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's becoming a little more complicated now. Was Zeljo Puselja wounded at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was wounded in the right arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not on the rib? He was not wounded on the rib?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Zeljo Puselja was not wounded on the rib. He was wounded in the arm, and Darko Puselja was wounded in the rib and the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Darko Puselja was. Thank you so much. Thank you very much, Madam Sartorio. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, that's okay, Your Honour. I need to go back. It appears in the record -- I thought that the witness had mentioned the name of the kid, and we can either go back to the record or I'll just ask him if he knows the name of the kid he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the kid that you have been referring to?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The one that had not been wounded? Pavo Barac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And could you tell us how old he was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was not older than 16 at the time. I think he was 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: On the map, sir, could you draw the line that shows the route that you took and then draw a number "9" where the incident -- where you dressed your wounds?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Should I draw a line leading towards the figure, or what do you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. From number 8, did you just go straight across to number 9, or just indicate for the record the direction that you went in.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were moving from this figure 8 to figure 9. That was the direction, and that's where we dressed our wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then from 9, which direction did you go in?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then from figure 9, we moved towards the village of Fazlici and there is the village of Orasac. I can't see it here. This is where we spent one day and one night in a pine wood, and then we went to Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what happened in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we were at Orasac, we thought that we could be saved once we reached Guca Gora, because at that time we didn't know that Guca Gora had already been captured, that it had fallen. We moved at around 9.00 or 8.00 -- 9.00 or 10.00 from Orasac to Guca Gora, and we reached Guca Gora at around 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. We saw that there was nobody there, that all the houses were deserted. And as it got light, we realised that we shouldn't be there, and we went towards Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I realise that these places aren't on the map, but can you tell us, in relation to Fazlici, where Guca Gora is, if it's to the north or to the east?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: East or northeast, I really can't tell you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far in kilometres it is?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: From Fazlici? From Orasac or Fazlici?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Fazlici.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the road goes through Donje Maline, and maybe five or six kilometres, five, six kilometres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe Map number 9 might be able to help you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But we need to capture this image on this map first before we move; otherwise, we lose the image. Thank you. May that be entered as an exhibit as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map on the screen is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 129.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, do you want to conduct the questioning or would you like me to ask the witness about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. You carry on, and I guess you're about five minutes from your hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have just two more questions, Your Honour, as soon as we can get to when the witness arrived at safety. Could you put up Map 9, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While we are looking for the next map, Mr. Witness, can I ask you if, at the time you were fleeing off the next day from Guca Gora, were you then by that time alone with the kid? There was only two of you or were there others from the original group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was just the two of us, and the other three were captured at Postinje, where we were trying to bind our wounds. These two men managed to capture them, and we were the only ones who managed to flee towards Fazlic and then to Orasac, where we spent this one night and one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the map in front of you, do you see Guca Gora on this map?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would you circle it, please, and put a number "1"?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Should I circle the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry. Just put a number "1."

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was this your final destination?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We moved on towards the village of Kula, towards Nova Bila, in fact, but we encountered a soldier there. I think he was a BH Army soldier. He was there on the hill, and we were in the meadow and we ran through a grove. And he suddenly stood up in front of us, and we didn't dare to proceed forward. So we moved back to Guca Gora, where we made a plan. We wanted to go by way of Vlasic out of Guca Gora. We saw that there were many soldiers there, however; and then we moved towards Han Bila. There is a Croat village there Kosovo; and then as we moved to Han Bila, two men, two soldiers saw us from Guca Gora and they ran after us. And then as we walked towards Han Bila, from a grove shots were fired at us, so we went to the village of Sarici. We went right, took a right turn. There was a Croat flag flying in the village of Sarici. There were three soldiers up there on the hill. And we saw that this was the HVO, and I knew a man from Guca Gora. His name was Zlaja, that's the name I knew him by. And they asked us what happened, and then we told them; and then I was transferred to the Nova Bila hospital to get treatment for my wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever contacted by anyone from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina about this incident?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you ever give a statement to the news media?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I may have been interviewed by the BBC. I think it was in 1993, maybe two or three days after the events.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you ever give a statement to any human rights organisation about what happened to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I made two statements of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know if one statement was recorded?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the BBC guys -- well, I don't know what they did, how they went about it. We were in front of a house, and that was all very short. I never saw any of the footage or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your interviews or your statement that you gave to human rights organisation, do you know if that statement was audio-recorded?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd like to just play 30 seconds of a tape, to see if the witness can identify anything on the tape. We have to do it in closed session because it's an international organisation, Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Before we do that, you're going to do something about the map on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Your Honour. I would like to freeze that map and enter it as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That map is entered as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This is the last question I have, Your Honour, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the tape to come on, could you tell me approximately --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We have to go into private session at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Marijanovic. My name is Nicholas Robson, and I'll be asking you some questions for the Defence this afternoon. Mr. Marijanovic, I'm a little bit unclear about your last answers. It's right, is it not, that on the 12th of June, just some four days after the incident in Bikosi, you gave a statement about what happened to some international human rights officers. Do you remember meeting with international human rights officers?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you remember going to the HQ of the British Battalion in Vitez soon after the events of 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you spoke with some members of the International Community whilst you were there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is it possible that those officers recorded what you said or took a statement of what you told them?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think they did, but I don't remember, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. You've confirmed that there were other occasions when you gave statements about what happened at Maline and Bikosi; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some statements. I don't think that they were recorded or written down anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, do you remember attending at the Human Rights Centre in Medjugorje in October of 1993? Have you heard of that Human Rights Centre, first of all?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I've never heard of it, and I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: How about the Commission for the Verification of War Crimes in the Treaty of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; have you ever heard of that commission?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about any of those commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, you've never heard of the Human Rights Centre at Medjugorje, and you've never heard of the Commission for the Verification of War Crimes?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did hear about this Human Rights Centre, but I wasn't in Medjugorje. I didn't go to Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You can confirm, however, that you were interviewed by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you gave a statement to that investigator in September of the year 2000; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that your memory of the events at Maline and Bikosi would be much better than when you gave -- when you gave that statement back in 2000 than it is now some 14 years after the event; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That the statement was better? Well, I wouldn't agree with that, because I was dazed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: At what time were you dazed?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the first statement that I gave, I was depressed. My wife and children were in captivity. I didn't know anything about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You see, I would suggest to you that you've given several statements, at least three, if not more. You're mentioning now that you were dazed. Let's be clear. Are you saying you were dazed when you gave the statement to the OTP investigator in September 2000?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, I was fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So your recollection of the events would have been clear [Realtime transcript read in error "clearer"] at the time you gave your statement to the investigator; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. Clearer than what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I said "clear" rather than clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, it's written down "clearer."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify that, the question I asked you: Your recollection of the events relating to Maline and Bikosi would have been clear when you gave your statement to the investigator in September of the year 2000; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to the events at the start of the war that you spoke about. It's right that in March 1992, the Serb forces had started digging trenches around your village of Paklarevo and in the general area of the Travnik Municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And those Serbs had set up positions upon Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the edge of Vlasic, yes, in the direction of Travnik and Turbe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In May 1992, you yourself were hit by mortar shrapnel, and you were wounded, seriously wounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't one piece but ten pieces of shrapnel. A shell landed right behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And while you were recovering, you and your family moved to Maline village, which is also in Travnik Municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the reason you went there was because Maline village was quieter. There was not --

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was further away from the Serb positions, so I thought it was better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Maline village is made up of two parts, isn't it? Gornje Maline, the upper part, is where the Croats lived; and Donje Maline, the lower part, is where the Bosnian Muslims lived; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you moved to Maline village, at that time, both the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats had organised separate defensive lines facing towards the Serbs on Mount Vlasic; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned Mujahedin in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you first saw them in the Travnik Municipality at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw small groups of Mujahedin. From that, do I take it, that there was more than one group of Mujahedin in the area, in the Travnik Municipality?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, around that time, is it right to say that you noticed some of the local Bosnian Muslims join the members of the Arab Mujahedin and started copying their appearance; for example, they started growing beards and wearing similar clothing to the Mujahedin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that happened, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In the spring of 1993, once you'd moved to Maline village, it's right, isn't it, that tensions between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims started to increase, the relations deteriorated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it right that around March 1993, a new Croatian Defence Council brigade was formed in your area and had a headquarters at the Guca Gora monastery?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know much about that. It's possible, because there was an HVO, and I'm sure they had a command somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you recall most of the Bosnian Croat men from your village and around the area who were fit for military service became members of that brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And soon after the establishment of that brigade, is it right to say that the HVO members from Maline village started establishing military positions facing the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina set up lines towards them, and they set up lines towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, at that point in time, is it right to say that the members of the Croatian Defence Council from Maline and the surrounding villages no longer went to the defensive lines on Vlasic, facing the Serbs, but now went to the new positions around their village, facing towards the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know much about that because I didn't go to the lines. I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Let's turn to the events on the 8th of June. You've told us that an attack commenced between 4.00 and 5.00 that day, and it was launched by the Bosnian Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You said the attack lasted for some ten hours, until the Bosnian Army took the village; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And there were a large number of HVO soldiers located around Maline village that day, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And those HVO soldiers tried to defend the village from the Bosnian Army attack, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, when the Bosnian Army managed to take the village, it's correct to say that some of the HVO soldiers were able to escape towards Guca Gora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, towards Guca Gora and Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you've explained to the Court that during the attack you were in the cellar of your -- it your brother's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the house of my wife's brother. My family house, where I was born, was far away from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you spent most of the time during the attack in the cellar with your family and also your wife's brother's family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, at around midday, somebody from the Bosnian Army shouted for all the Bosnian Croat villagers to come out of the houses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You, yourself, noticed some villagers coming out of the houses and surrendering, and then you decided to come out and surrender as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you came out of the house with your family, and you met up with the other Bosnian Croats in a yard in front of a house in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When the Bosnian Army troops rounded up the Bosnian Croat villagers, it's fair to say that they treated you properly, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when the Bosnian Army gathered you all together, that was in the center of the village and you gathered together with other Bosnian Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not all of them, but with some of them apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your evidence, you've mentioned that you gathered together with 40 or 50 people, is that right, civilians, you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can I suggest to you that amongst that group there were also Bosnian Croat soldiers who were wearing uniform as well?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's right. At this stage, one of the Bosnian Army soldiers ordered your group to start walking towards Mehurici; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, in your group at that time, how many people were there? About 40 or 50?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, about that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you walked from Gornje Maline all the way to Poljanice village, escorted by three or four Bosnian Army soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You actually passed through Poljanice village and continued in the direction of Mehurici; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that it was at that point that you came across another group of 15 to 19 Croat men walking in the opposite direction, towards the direction of Bikosi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, that group of Bosnian Croat men, they were escorted by some other people, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right to say, isn't it, that the men, the persons escorting the Bosnian Croats, were four Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were both Mujahedin and members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who spoke Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, that's not right, is it? Those men, escorting those Bosnian Croats, there were two foreign men and two local Mujahedin; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the local Mujahedin, you mentioned, had green masks on their faces and they looked like ninjas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: They weren't dressed like ordinary Bosnian Army soldiers, were they?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Some were and some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, those four men, who I've described as Mujahedin, they stopped your group, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding that you were towards the back of your group, so you had difficulties in seeing what was going on exactly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you help us with this: Those four men that I have described as Mujahedin, it's right, isn't it, that they threatened the Bosnian Army soldiers that were escorting your group with their weapons?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They -- I don't know what they did among themselves; but when they separated off 12, they had some kind of misunderstanding. But what it was about, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, those four men, they separated the men, you've mentioned six or seven men, from your group of Bosnian Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They separated off about 12 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the 12 men that they separated from the group, were they all of military service age?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, will that be a convenient time or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've certainly got plenty more questions, so I think that is good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can imagine. So this would be as good a time to stop as any other?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourns to tomorrow at 9.00 in Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
